speechtext:
I hope that it will come by the end of next week. Recommendations on behalf of this bill have been made by judicial officers. The bill relates to the trial of j'oung persons. Under the Juvenile Delinquents Act the parents have to be notified, and the magistrate or the judge has a procedure to go through prior to and after the trial of the delinquents. My proposal is to extend these provisions, the wisdom of which in times like these has been demonstrated, to those under nineteen years of age. As I stated in moving the first reading of this bill, many people who are in trouble- some among the most dangerous criminals we have-are of about that age. The class I have in mind, however, is the high school element that are out of work through no fault of their own, and many of whose parents axe on relief. As a result they go to new Ontario, where, having no references, they cannot get a job. I have before me a letter from a commercial traveller who lives in the riding of the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Massey). My correspondent, who is a reputable commercial man, upon a recent trip through' new Ontario visited Sudbury, Kirkland Lake, Timmins and other mining centres. "At Kirkland Lake," he states, "twenty Canadian young men were locked up and given eight days in gaol on vagrancy charges. These boys were only looking for work. And we call this a free country. Let
3328	COMMONS
Criminal Code-Trial of Young Persons
any young Canadian go to one of the ore mining centres and seek work and see what he will get."
Many children who are to-day in factories should be in school, and nearly all the young offenders come from poverty stricken homes, where the father is out of work. They have never had a real chance. Many of them are handicapped since birth through insufficient food and clothing; too often, when the father is on relief, the eldest boy leaves home and goes to new Ontario or other places, and the only charge that can be laid against him is that he cannot get work. Section 238, the vagrancy section of the criminal code, states:
Every one is a loose, idle or disorderly person or vagrant who,-
(a)	not having any visible means of subsistence, is found wandering abroad or lodging in any barn or outhouse, et cetera.
Lads like these are the forgotten element under the constitution.
By this bill I do not intend to place any additional expense upon the public. As I said in moving first reading, in the larger cities there are many bodies such as the Lions Club, the Big Brother movement, the Big Sister movement and so on, all engaged in helping in this work and willing to help still more. Right here in the city of Ottawa we have the Lions Club, which has been helping in this work for some time past. I repeat that the parents or other next of kin should be notified. When these children get into trouble they do not want their parents notified, and in many cases as a result wind up serving a term in gaol, and come out with that stigma attached to them. I do not want to criticize the magistrates, but only a couple of weeks ago two of these young fellows were arrested in New Toronto. They were eighteen years of age, and when the magistrate said, ''Supposing I give you three months in the reformatory," one of them replied, "It doesn't matter to me." The magistrate said: "So you've reached the indifferent stage. I don't wonder at it. Where is your home?" The boys replied that their home originally had been in Winnipeg but that they had been just roaming around for the lost four years. Accepting their statement that they had never been in trouble before, the magistrate gave them ten days each. The only complaint against them was that they were trying to get work, and that is the sort of thing that goes on. Many of these people are sent down without even being heard. It is not the fault of the magistrates; it is the system that is to blame. All I ask is that when the minister considers the amendments to the criminal code he should also consider extending the

provisions of the Juvenile Delinquents Act to those under nineteen years of age, especially those of the high school population. Only the other day at the Union station in Toronto -and I saw this myself when the train was about to leave for Ottawa in the morning- twenty-one of these young people were brought back from new Ontario, some of them were charged with vagrancy and all being brought to the Guelph reformatory because there was no room for them in the gaols in northern Ontario. Their only crime was that they could not find jobs. After checking up on the stories of some of these cases of young people the police often find that they had never been in trouble before, but they simply could not get work.
I do not ask anything out of the way. I believe this problem should be dealt with as it is in England to-day, where many of the prisons have been closed. This problem has been brought about very largely by the depression. I have before me the blue book of the Inspector of Prisons for the province of Ontario which shows that these conditions are largely due to the depression, and when the depression is over no doubt they will vanish. But the state has a duty to give these youths a fair trial, and if they are not represented by counsel there are in the large centres service clubs that could take care of such matters. Many lawyers are doing such work for nothing, and I only ask the minister to look into this matter. If he can give it any attention when the criminal code is being amended I hope he will do so, because I know some of these high school children of the city of Toronto who have got into trouble through no fault of their own; they were only looking for work in new Ontario and other places.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISIONS GOVERNING TRIAL OF YOUNG PERSONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend has suggested that this matter should be considered and a decision rendered before the introduction of the general bill concerning the criminal code, but only this afternoon I heard him complain that we were asking too much when we took time to study things and did not reach decisions. I have reached a decision as far as this bill is concerned; I am compelled to oppose it and to ask that it should not pass.
May I say, Mr. Speaker, that the provisions of the Juvenile Delinquents Act are the result of very careful work and deliberations on the part of the child welfare council, which is composed of philanthropic people all over Canada who are deeply interested in the work. Some of the members of that council are magistrates who have had long experience with regard to

Criminal Code-Trial oj Young Persons
the procedure concerning children. I was minister in charge of the act when it was put through some years ago, after a meeting of that council, and I would hesitate to change some of the important provisions of that act merely because my hon. friend thinks they should be changed. According to this act a child is defined as follows:
"Child" means any boy or girl apparently or actually under the age of sixteen years: provided, that in any province or provinces as to which the governor in council by proclamation has directed or may hereafter direct, "child" means any boy or girl apparently or actually under the age of eighteen years: provided further, that any such proclamation may apply either to boys only or to girls only or to both boys and girls.
Three provinces, British Columbia, Manitoba and Alberta, by resolution of their governments have asked that the governor in council should raise the age to eighteen, so in those provinces when boys or girls under eighteen years of age are arrested they are classed as juvenile delinquents under the act and treated in that special way. This request has not been made by the other provinces; indeed, in at least one province the lieutenant governor in council has asked that there should be no change as far as that province is concerned. Various bodies in some of the provinces have asked that the age should be raised to eighteen, but the federal government has always required that this request should be made by the governmental authorities of the province, by the lieutenant governor in council. So in three of the provinces at least the notices, which my hon. friend would require to be given to the parents, are given as far as children under eighteen years of age are concerned.
My hon. friend wants the provisions of section 10 of the Juvenile Delinquents Act, which requires notice to be given to the parents or to friends of the parents before a juvenile delinquent is tried, to apply to children between the ages of sixteen and nineteen, and in the second place his bill demands that counsel should be appointed by the court to defend such juvenile delinquents. As I have said, with respect to the first provision, in three provinces it would not be needed, because there the age has been raised to eighteen. As far as the other provinces are concerned I believe this would have the effect of delaying the trials of those nineteen years of age or under, especially when there are no relatives in the city or town where they have been arrested and where their trial will be held. If notice should be sent to relatives elsewhere and an investigation should be carried on to find them, I do not think it would be in the
interests of justice or even of the boys themselves that their trial should be delayed as long as would be required for that purpose. When the relatives are in the city where the trial takes place it must be exceptional if they do not know of or are not made acquainted with the troubles in which their children are involved.
I do not agree with the statement of my hon. friend, which is also in the explanatory note attached to his bill, that many young people are being sent to gaol in a mechanical way. I think that is a terrible indictment of Canadian courts, and one that is neither fair nor justified. It is certainly not in accordance with any reports received by the Department of Justice. On the contrary I believe that our judges everywhere take special care when the delinquents who are brought before them are young people. Surely my hon. friend could not substantiate that charge against the courts of Canada, that they are simply throwing away boys and girls, sending them to gaol mechanically without proper trial.
If we are to raise the age under which boys and girls are to be considered as children and come under the provisions of the Juvenile Delinquents Act I think this should be done with the cooperation of the provinces. The provinces are more directly interested in this matter. The age limit as at present set is the limit asked for by the child welfare council, and before any change is made I would like to have their views about it, as well as the views of the provinces.
With regard to the proposal that counsel should be supplied for the defence of juvenile delinquents, and even those who are no longer juvenile but under the age of nineteen, that would constitute a considerable change and, if it were made, surely a demand would follow that this should be done in all cases. If it is the provinces that would have to pay for the defending counsel we should at least consult with them before putting that provision into our statutes. The administration of justice is under provincial jurisdiction. If my hon. friend has in mind that this should be an expense of the dominion government, that might be considered, but I think his bill would be ultra vires as far as that goes because it would be a charge on the treasury of the country and so my hon. friend would have no right to introduce such a bill.
On the whole, in spite of all that is said and suggested in the introduction of this bill, I think Canadian justice is not so bad, and many things that have been said are not
Bank oj Canada

justified. The courts of the country take great care when it comes to the trial of young people. I do not think the change suggested by this bill is necessitated by any condition which exists at the present time. Therefore, as I said, I am sorry, but I do not feel justified in accepting this bill, and I oppose its second reading.

subtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OP CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before I proceed: to a discussion of the features of the resolution of which I wish to speak, I want to correct some statements that were made this afternoon by the hon. member for St. Antoine-Westmount (Mr. White). If I recall his remarks correctly he suggested, first, that there is an abundance of money available and that there is no shortage of funds for all proper needs of the public. In support of that extraordinary statement he suggested as evidence the fact that there is something over $2,000,000,000 of bank deposits and less than $1,000,000,000 of current loans, and while he did not say so, the inference was left that apparently there are bank deposits available for financing Canadian activities to the extent of roughly $1,500,000,000.
May I place on record the actual facts as at the end of 1935. Our bank deposits consisted of the following items:	Deposits
in foreign countries, $348,000,000; current accounts, that is accounts on which cheques may be drawn every day in the transaction of the commerce of the country and upon which the banks do not pay any interest because they do not treat them as loanable deposits, $568,000,000; time or savings accounts, which are withdrawable only on notice to the banks, and upon which the banks pay interest, $1,445,000,000. As against those savings bank deposits the banks had out current loans of $828,000,000, and in addition to that they had advanced on account of national, provincial, municipal, railway loans and other public securities the sum of $1,175,000,000. Besides that there were call loans outstanding totalling $82,000,000, making a total of investments by the banks in Canada of $2,085,000,000. If we subtract these savings deposits from the amount the banks

had actually invested in that type of security we find that the banks had invested $640,000,000 more than the total of savings deposits.
But that does not tell the whole story. In addition to the $2,085,000,000 invested in the type of loan and security I have mentioned, the other investments of the chartered banks totalled $900,000,000. As a matter of fact, to-day the total volume of our bank credit currency, our bank note currency, our Bank of Canada currency and our metal currency is roughly about 50 per cent below where it would be had the same ratio of advancement been sustained from 1915 to 1935 that had obtained from 1867 to 1915. Since 1918 there has been a steady decrease in the total volume of money available for the Canadian people. The hon. member went a little further and suggested that when Reginald McKenna, not only a banker but a man who for many years was one of the most distinguished chancellors of the exchequer who had ever graced the British House of Commons, said that the banks make deposits by calling bank loans deposits he was talking utter nonsense. Not only has that distinguished statesman and banker in England made that statement, but it is recorded as the unanimous conclusion of the British Macmillan commission, the report of which has been properly described by Sir Josiah Stamp as the outstanding book on modern practical monetary and political economy. Not only have the Macmillan commission confirmed the statement, but similar statements have been made by Carl Snyder possibly one of the most distinguished economists and statisticians in the employ of the federal reserve banking system. It has recently been made definitely by one who graces the high position of chairman of the board of governors of the federal reserve system of the United States, Mr. Marriner Eccles. In addition to that group of distinguished authorities, the facts speak for themselves.
I have pointed out to the committee that to-day there are so-called bank deposits in Canada totalling $2,361,000,000, and deducting the amount of foreign deposits, or deposits in branches of Canadian banks operating abroad, the amount is something over $2,000,000,000. How much money have we in Canada? We have created by law under the Currency Act metal coin to the value of $39,000,000. We have bills issued by the Bank of Canada under the authority of the Bank of Canada Act, amounting to $99,000,000; we have bank bills, issued under the Bank Act by chartered banks, amounting to $135,000,000, and we have foreign currency in the possession of our Canadian banks, totalling $21,000,000. In all, the entire

Bank oj Canada
money wealth of Canada is $294,000,000. If we take that $294,000,000 from the $2,361,000,000 the bankers claim they have on deposit, we have the amount of bank deposits in excess of the total money in issue and in circulation in this dominion.
In other words the bankers have created, in excess of the money that exists in the dominion, bank deposits to a total of $2,067,000,-
000.	How was that money created? It was created by the simple process which modern banking practice has adopted of substituting bank credit created by a bookkeeping system, and issued as money fictitiously called bank deposits-mere statements of accounts which are promises to pay, money which does not exist in the country and which the banker cannot meet if he is ever called upon to meet it. I do not know if anybody else can do that kind of thing without going to the penitentiary. I challenge the government or the Department of Justice to find in our currency or banking legislation a single authority or provision which sanctions the principle that our chartered banks are following, namely that of trading short in money. I am inclined to the opinion

and I speak not only as a member of parliament but as a lawyer who has given some little time and thought to this subject-that this is the greatest unchallenged swindle and vicious exploitation of the egregious principle of trading short that is to be found in any department of the mad activities inspired by the pursuit of profit. I was amused w'hen the hon. member for St. Antoine-Westmount spoke sympathetically about the capacity of banking institutions to earn profits. I have checked the figures and I find that in 1934, on a capital investment of $144,000,000, the banks made an actual profit of $18,000,000 which figures out roughly to 12 per cent-not bad for a depression year. But that was not all. That profit was paid out by the Bank of Montreal at the rate of 8 per cent, a decrease from 1930 when they paid 14 per cent. The other banks ranged from 6 per cent to 12 per cent, but the average stood at about 12 per cent; then they put aside as rest account an amount almost as great. Last year, in 1935, their profits were a little better, and the preliminary dividend paid by the Bank of Montreal in the first quarter of this year, 1936, is, I believe, four per cent, indicating that the depression is not going to put our banks out of business so far as taking care of themselves is concerned, because with that profit and with the reduction in the interest rate on deposits probably we shall see our banks weather the storm.
I am sorry that I was not in the house yesterday to listen to the speech of the hon.
Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning), but I should like to put part of his statement on the record to interpret what I think this resolution really means. As reported at page 3257 of Hansard, he said:
I should like now to discuss the factors which have led the government to propose amendments to the constitution of the bank providing for a predominant interest by the public in the ownership and also voting control of the bank. In the first place, the fundamental consideration is that the primary function of a central bank is to regulate the volume of currency and credit in use, and this is so vital a national function that it should not be left to the control of private interests. The issue of currency has always been regarded as a prerogative of the crown. It ic true that in all modern countries during the growth and development of banking practice, the use of bank notes, and particularly of cheques drawn against bank deposits, has come largely to supplant in the business world the use of hand to hand currencies. The significance of this amazing development of bank credits as the chief form of purchasing power was not at first perceived, and it is only in comparatively recent times that governmental authorities and monetary experts-and indeed central bankers themselves-have come to realize that the primary function of a central bank was not to make loans to a necessitous government or to provide other banking services but rather to control the volume of credit and currency in the best interests of the economic life of the nation.
Well, if that is the power of the central bank it means that in that bank's authority is the right to control the economic progress of the people of the nation, which means that in that bank is vested control over the government's right to set and maintain an advancing standard of living for the people. The hon. Minister of Finance went on:
But the point is that for the first time in this country we have an institution which is charged with the function of regulating credit and currency, and which therefore will conscientiously and deliberately-

Consciously, not conscientiously. I am glad to have that correction because I am sure they would not do it conscientiously. I do not blame the minister for correcting that slip. He went on:
-and which therefore will consciously and deliberately set influences to work which will affect the price level as well as the level of production, trade and employment. Surely this is too vital a function to leave in the hands of a privately controlled institution.
Well, it has been there for some time, and we know something about the state of the price level and about trade and economic conditions and the state of unemployment in the nation. He went on:
If this function is to be performed at all it should only be by an institution under
Bank of Canada

adequate government control. This is my main point, Mr. Chairman; in fact it is the sum and substance of the whole matter.
A little later on, carrying the same line of reasoning right to the issue of national policy, he quoted with approval the expressions of the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in this wise:
I am however, discussing the question of control of policy, and I do say that with respect to policies, whether they relate to trade, to shipping, to marketing, to finance, to defence, or to any other phase of a country's economy, those policies, if they are the expression of view of a government representative of the people, should be capable of being carried out without interference from any institution whatever.
Then in the course of the debate, as reported at page 3298 of Hansard, this quotation from the Prime Minister was read':
The Liberal party believes that credit is a public matter, not of interest to bankers only, but of direct concern to the average citizen. It stands for the immediate establishment of a properly constituted national central bank, to perform the functions of rediscount, and the control of currency issue, considered in terms of public need. A central bank is necessary to determine the supply of currency in relation to the domestic, social and industrial requirements of the Canadian people; and also to deal with problems of international commerce and exchange.
And this discussion followed:
Mr. Mackenzie King: What is wrong with that?
Mr. Douglas: There is nothing wrong with it. What we are asking for now is legislation to implement that.
Mr. Dunning: It is before the committee.
If that is true, no one can have any fault to find with the proposed resolution, but I cannot bring myself to believe that the adoption of the principle of a partly privately owned, partly publicly owned, Bank of Canada is in conformity with the declared acknowledgment that the bank controls the economic life of the nation and has the power to regulate its currency and credit, or that it is not vesting in this Bank of Canada a power which will enable it, if it wills, to interfere with the government in matters of national policy.
Let me put the matter to the committee on a plain, simple arithmetical basis. We now meet a situation where it is proposed to continue five million dollars' worth of shareholders in the Bank of Canada. They are to have the right to vote seven votes, through their representatives on the board of directors. The government vests its authority in a governor and deputy governor and gives four of its directors double voting power, or eight votes. Very well. Let us assume that three

of the directors appointed by the government decide to vote with the seven directors representing the shareholders, and who can guarantee in face of the argument presented by the Minister of Railways (Mr. Howe) for the removal of the Canadian National Railway trustees, that the appointees of this government are going to conform with the wishes of the government and that they are not going to conform with the wishes of five million dollars' worth of shareholders?
How far then are we going to carry out the promises that were made, absolutely, not assurances that were given as a mere idle message to the people in the heat of a campaign, but promises that were recorded upon the pages of parliamentary history in the House of Commons by the Liberal party as it made its stand before it went to the last election in its appeal to the electorate? Of course, I feel strongly on this issue. I may have been over-optimistic; I may have been unwarrantably enthusiastic in my conclusion that Liberalism was going to establish, over the oligarchy of money power that long had ruled this and other countries, the supreme sovereignty of parliament and of democracy by restoring to parliament the constitutional right, yes, may I go further and say, the constitutional duty to create the currency and credit media of exchange which were necessary to sustain government and the progress of humanity. I may have been over-optimistic in my belief that the day was going to dawn when Liberalism would usher in an era when mankind in this country would be emancipated from the slavery of debt and from the bondage of usury. And I do not believe that that promise is being fulfilled.
Now, may I say a word by way of reminder, because I want to warn the government and the Liberal party to-day that if I am right in my conclusions as to the way in which the public has interpreted these promises that were made while the government was in opposition, and that were made as a pledge before the election, if they are not fulfilled then it may be that the Liberal party is placing its footsteps on that trail of broken promises which leads not only through the valley of humiliation but down deep into the abysmal depths of eternal oblivion.
Now I may be pardoned if for a moment I refer to a distinguished chancellor of the exchequer who went through the experience of restoring the gold standard money system to Great Britain. When the Right Hon. Winston Churchill, standing in his place as Chancellor of the British Exchequer in 1925, recommended the restoration of the very kind of

Batik of Canada
system which the Bank of Canada Act has adopted, and promised the people of Great Britain the security which it offered, on the assurance that every expert commission and every authoritative source of administration worth listening to had declared for the necessity of returning to the gold standard, he did, of course, enter the valley of oblivion and, in his case, not without very much humiliation, because he bobbed up in the British House of Commons in 1936 with probably one of the most profound acknowledgments of imperfect action, which had been corrected by time, that had ever been made. In 1936 he says:
Great Britain has shaken herself free from the Gladstonian structure and tradition of finance. Now, he said, we are a protectionist nation with a substantial tariff, which we should no doubt raise higher as the years go by. The gold standard was not only dead, but had been relegated for a long period to purgatory. We have no sinking fund except a small fortuitous balance of the last year's surplus. We have dealt with the American debt liability in a manner which nobody would have tolerated in the years when I was chancellor.
A significant feature of Mr. Churchill's address will be found, I think, in the fact that he acknowledges that under the direction of the classical economy and orthodox finance of the nineteenth century his 1925 policy of deflation, which I venture to say is being more or. less carried out by this type of legislation and by our own budget this year, a budget balanced through reduction in public expenditure and increased taxation, brought England to disaster. To save herself she was compelled to resort to managed currency, industrial bonuses, protection of home industry, regulation of trade and commerce, public works and social services; and in fact, on his authority-and no one is in a better position to speak than he is-the way to recovery is to be found, first, in the abandonment of the classical, orthodox school of economy and finance of the Victorian era, and, second, in the adoption of a policy based upon all that has been denounced in the past as unsound. He added this touch, which I think is interesting: After relegating the gold standard and orthodox, classical economists to the place in hell from which they came, and wholly justifying the complete repudiation of the ideas of that classical, orthodox economy and finance, which he formerly championed, he said:
All those rules by which chancellors of every party, except in war time, were rigidly bound, have now been swept away. How former chancellors would stare, if what has been done could all be explained to them, he said, as he blandly referred to himself as "the last orthodox chancellor of the Victorian epoch."
Amidst cheers and laughter he appealed to the committee "to recognize me as the last of the Mohicans."
I am afraid that Mr. Churchill cannot have that privilege, because apparently the effect of the retreats in the Ottawa valley, which I believe was not altogether a land of the Mohicans but rather a land of the Iroquois, has been to produce another chancellor, a chancellor of the Canadian exchequer, who has really stuck solidly by the thing which brought Churchill to disaster in 1925.

Read your Bank of Canada Act. Let us see what Churchill said in 1925. I expected this. He said:
During the late administration, late Chancellor of the Exchequer (Mr. Snowden) appointed a committee of experts and high authorities to examine into the question of the amalgamation of the treasury and the Bank of England note issues.

We thus resume our international position as a gold standard country. That is an important event, but I hasten to add a qualification. Returning to the international gold standard does not mean that we are going to issue gold coinage. That is quite unnecessary for the purpose of the gold standard, and is out of the question in present circumstances. It would be an unwarrantable extravagance which our present financial stringency by no means allows us to indulge in. Indeed, I must appeal to all classes in the public interest to continue to use notes and to make no change in the habits and practices they have become used to for the last ten years. The practice of the last ten year's has protected the Bank of England and other banks against any appreciable demand for sovereigns or half sovereigns. But now that we are returning publicly to the gold standard in international matters with a

free export gold, I feel that it will be better for us to regularize what has been our practice by legislation. I shall therefore propose to introduce a bill which, among other things, will provide the following:

Secondly. That the right to tender bullion to the mint to be coined shall be confined in the future by law, as it has long been confined in practice, to the Bank of England.

speechtext:
The house resumed consideration, in committee of the proposed resolution with respect to the Bank of Canada-Mr. Dunning-Mr. Sanderson in the chair.
Mr. MeGEER:	The main point the committee is considering is not merely a change in the form of ownership of the stock of the Bank of Canada. That is simply incidental to the establishment of control over the creation and issue of the currency needs of both government and people in the Dominion of Canada. The issue that came up in the last election campaign, and that I think was stressed more than anything else, was a plain and simple one:	Shall parliament
delegate its power to create by law and put into circulation the currency and credit which constitute the media of the exchange needs of both government and people, and issue the currency and credit media of exchange in terms of public need, or shall they be subject to the limitation of being issued in terms of private gain. That issue is fundamental to the establishment of a new era of ordered progress. If we fail to meet our promise to the electors of Canada in that regard we shall fail to fulfil a promise which amounted to a guarantee to bring about a fundamental change in the practical political economy that governed parliament in the past, under which social and economic security disappeared and poverty and destitution became the order of the day after education and science had created circumstances under which we should have looked forward to unbounded progress and prosperity.
I do not know that there is any need to hurry with a matter so fundamentally important to the well-being of future generations. To-day we are carrying a debt load of nine and a half billion dollars created

Bank oj Canada
under the private money system which has persistently issued currency and credit in terms of private gain. If we are going to make a change that is going to save humanity from an appalling calamity, then we as a parliament should take time to give full and mature consideration to this matter. I am going to suggest to the government that it is unfortunate that a measure of such great importance should have been introduced in what are now recognized as the closing days of this session of parliament, and I am going to ask the government to accept the following amendment, which is moved by myself and seconded by the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens):
That this resolution be referred to a select committee of parliament consisting of six members of the senate and seven members of the House of Commons, and that such committee shall be empowered to investigate all matters relating to currency and credit, banking, finance and commerce and to prepare and present to parliament for its consideration at its next sitting a bill that will bring about the establishment of a properly constituted central bank through which shall be performed the functions of rediscount and the control of currency issue in terms of public need, not possible private gain, and through which the supply of currency and credit shall be determined in relation to the domestic, social and industrial requirements of the Canadian people.
Of course I know it is easy to say that in connection with these issues one should appreciate the plight of the government; that public opinion is not prepared for fundamental changes; that there may be difficulties in the Senate and even in the House of Commons. But one thing is certain; it is that the Liberal members of this house and the electorate throughout the Dominion of Canada have a right to know why the fulsome promises made by the then opposition when it opposed this Bank of Canada Act, and made to the electorate in connection with the establishment of a national central bank, properly constituted, that would be publicly owned and publicly operated, are now to be altered to mean a central bank partly owned by the public and partly owned privately, under which a hundred thousand $50 subscribers are given a preferred security at the rate of 44 per cent. By this resolution we tell these shareholders: We do not need your money and we will not let you have a voice in the management of the bank. Therefore all this resolution is doing, so far as the privately owned part of that banking institution is concerned, is creating a preference for a few on a 44 per cent investment basis, and establishing a power and an authority that may be
in a position to frustrate the government in the establishment and maintenance of national policy.
Believing as I sincerely do that this measure does not fulfil the fundamental promise that was made and that this government and the Liberal members of the house were elected to fulfil, I think time for consideration would be advisable, and I am sure that after due and proper consideration a greater change would be brought about in the right of the nation to control the issue of currency and credit than is contemplated in the legislation to be founded on this resolution.

The Minister of Justice a little while ago treated it as a frivolous matter. Now that we are back to the resolution I wish to make a very few observations.
It is frequently stated that the present or existing system of banking and finan/ce, in this instance the Bank of Canada or the general banking system or the financial system of the country, is to all intents and purposes a perfect system. That is, no suggestion of change should be entertained. But I have before me a brochure issued by the bankers' association in 1923, which contains some interesting matter. It will be recalled by the committee that in 1923 or 1924, I have forgotten which year, parliament amended the Bank Act so as to inaugurate a system of inspection of banks, and for the last twelve or thirteen years a system has been in operation which is and for many years has been recognized as a highly successful one. In the utterances of the bankers' association in 1923 I find these words:
Of all the proposed amendments to the Bank Act a system of government inspection will least stand the test of experience elsewhere and of common sense, and the plan is objectionable not from the standpoint of bankers and shareholders but of depositors who would inevitably be lulled into a false sense of security with a resultant demand upon the government when disaster occurs.
I cite that to indicate how futile and foolish is the tendency to pooh-pooh and ridicule any suggestion for change or progress. Here were the bankers who quite seriously, no doubt, declared that the proposal for bank inspection would not stand the test of experience or common sense. I was reminded of our venerable and very much beloved member from St. Antoine-Westmount (Mr. White) who this afternoon described as idiots those who hold that bank loans create bank deposits. He used the expression, "Who is there who would entertain such an idiotic idea?" Well, in the same brochure I find these words:
Nearly all loans are made by credits entered upon the books of the bank, or by cheques or drafts or acceptances, and these pass into the general clearing of the community of which only resulting balances are settled in money.
As far back as 1923 we find the bankers' association giving expression to the very suggestion that some people in this session of parliament regard1 as foolish and idiotic.
As the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. McGeer) so ably disclosed in his observations, it is the creation of credits by the banks which in large measure account for the rise in the deposits. There is nothing fictitious, nothing mysterious about the matter.
A man may go to a bank and borrow $1,000 on his own note of hand. The hon. member for St. Antoine-Westmount said that he might take the money and walk out. That is true; but quite likely he would pay it to some one for goods or services, and in that way the money would immediately return to the bank as deposits. What usually occurs is that the banker simply enters a credit to the individual borrowing, or if he secures his loan by the discounting of paper such as bills of exchange, notes of hand and so on, they are simply entered to his credit in the bank, and cheques issued against them.
I would suggest to the Minister of Finance that we might very well have a new column in bank annual or monthly statements showing the extent to which general deposits are accountable by loans. As a matter of fact a very substantial portion of general bank deposits-I am not speaking of savings deposits -are created in that way. There is no question about it. I remember reading a speech of one of the-

Mr. Chairman, as I said a few days ago, it is all very well for us to call this a free parliament, but unless a member is permitted to speak upon a resolution and1 if necessary to divide the house, parliament is not free and shows the need of constitutional and parliamentary reform. The present resolution is just what I would expect from the present government. From Vancouver to Halifax they have expressed different policies concerning the Bank of Canada. We know and have heard what the government's policy was in the Pacific province. A few days ago we heard what it was in Quebec and the maritimes, and notwith-

Bank oj Canada

standing what the Prime Minister may say I can tell the committee what it was in Ontario. In that province the policy of the government was one of straight public ownership; there is no doubt about that. They were going to get money from the bank to build breakwaters and harbours at the city of Toronto and elsewhere. Members of the Senate and House of Commons came to that city and indicated that they were going to use the Bank of Canada not only for ordinary banking purposes but for many other purposes. As I have said, the policy in each province was different. If I were asked my opinion I would say that the last state of the Bank of Canada is going to be worse than the first under this government. To-day the people of Canada are wondering what is going to become of the Bank of Canada. We spent a large amount of money on a royal commission in 1933, but before the bank has been functioning a year we turn the whole thing upside down and go back to where we were. I say, "God save the bank from its friends." In my humble opinion it will be a glorified Home Bank. As I said before, the government has got us into hot water in connection with the British North America Act, and I suggest that it would have been much better to leave the bank alone for a year or two in order to see how it would function.
A royal commission was appointed, but this resolution turns the report upside down. After the report was presented to parliament an act of parliament, being chapter 43 of the statutes of 1934, was enacted. I should like to point out the difference between the functions of the bank as indicated in the statute and the proposed new functions as indicated in the resolution, because they are as far apart as the poles. Yesterday, when it was indicated that the Prime Minister had stood for public ownership, he said that the interpretation was not a proper one, and explained that he wanted control, but not necessarily government ownership.
We have heard a great deal of talk about government control. When and where has it existed in Canada? Has it existed in connection with the railways? When was there a time when we had government control over anything or the tariff or the bankers' association, when has it existed since we have been a country? This resolution interferes with the whole scope of the Macmillan report. The Macmillan commission was appointed on July 31, 1933, to make an exhaustive inquiry as to whether we should have a central bank, and if so, whether it should be publicly or privately owned, or a combination of private and public ownership with the banks having
(Mr. Stevens.]
representation. Of the thirty-six countries that have central banks six countries, and some of the largest, have public ownership the Liberals were to pattern the Bank of Canada after the hydro-electric enterprise in Ontario; that was the shining example which Liberal candidates held up before the people in the last election-it was done here in Ontario-and they said that the Bank of Canada was to be a straight public ownership institution of that sort. Seventeen other countries have a central bank under private ownership. Eight countries have the ownership divided fifty-fifty between private and public ownership. There are a few others, mainly in Latin America, where the bank is partly privately and partly publicly owned, with the chartered banks having representation on the board.
Legislation was enacted on the basis of this Macmillan report. The chairman of the commission was the Right Hon. Lord Macmillan, and the commissioners were Sir Charles Stewart Addis, of London, England, Sir Thomas White, of Toronto, the Hon. J. E. Brownlee, of the province of Alberta, and Mr. Beaudry Leman, of the city of Montreal. As a result of the report of this commission parliament passed the Bank of Canada Act of 1934. The report of the Macmillan commission points out that the functions of a central bank are to regulate credit and currency; to regulate foreign exchange; to mitigate fluctuations in the level of production, trade, employment and prices as far as may be possible within the scope of monetary action, and to give expert financial advice to the government of the day. But what this resolution proposes is the direct opposite of what is proposed in the Macmillan report. The commission points out that the central bank should be a ready source of skilled and impartial financial advice at the disposal of the administration of the day. But this government does not want any technical advice.
This resolution is partly political and partly economic, and in the main, as I see it, it is political. At page 63 the Macmillan report says:
In return for the privileges which the state confers upon it-
That is, upon a central bank.
[DOT]-the bank should use its store of experience in the service of the community without the desire or the need to make profit a primary consideration.
I quote again from page 63:
The regulation of the quantity of credit is effected by the action of the central bank on the reserves of the commercial banks. By in-

Bank oj Canada
creasing or diminishing these reserves, or by increasing the cost of securing them, there is set in motion a process of expansion or contraction through the ordinary channels of banking. A central hank is thus not a competitor with the commercial banks. Its functions are regulatory and indirect.
That was the report of the commission, and the bank was created and opened its doors with a capital of $5,000,000, divided into $50 shares, which were offered for public subscription by the Minister of Finance on September 17, 1934. The offering was largely oversubscribed. The maximum allotment to any one individual or corporation was fifty shares. Shares of the bank may be held only by British subjects ordinarily resident in Canada, or by corporations controlled by British subjects ordinarily resident in Canada. The maximum holding permitted one person is fifty shares.
The bank is authorized to pay cumulative dividends of 4J per cent per annum on its profits, the remaining surplus to be paid, after making provision for bad and doubtful debts, depreciation in assets, pension fund and all such matters that are properly provided for by banks, into the consolidated revenue fund of Canada.
The bank may buy and sell securities of the dominion and the provinces. It may also buy and sell gold and silver, and may deal in foreign exchange.
The bank has assumed liability for dominion notes outstanding and is replacing them with its own notes in denominations of $1, $2, $5, $10, $20, $50, $100, $500 and $1,000. The chartered banks are required to reduce the issue of their own bank notes to 25 per cent of their paid-up capital during the next ten years.
The Bank of Canada must retain a reserve of gold equal to not less than 25 per cent of its total note and deposit liabilities in Canada.
The bank has an obligation to sell gold in the form of bars on demand.
The chartered banks are required to maintain a reserve of not 'less than five per cent of their deposit liabilities within Canada in the form of deposits with and notes of the bank.
The central bank acts as the fiscal agent of the Dominion of Canada and may by agreement act as banker or fiscal agent of any province. The bank must not accept deposits from individuals, and thus cannot compete with the chartered banks in commercial banking fields.

The governor of the bank is its chief executive officer, and he is assisted by a deputy governor and an assistant deputy governor. The first governors were appointed by the government and are as follows: Governor G. F. Towers, and the government were very lucky to get a man of his great ability, integrity and capacity. The deputy governor is J. A. C. Osborne, and the assistant deputy governor, L. P. St-Amour, good men. Subsequent appointments are to be made by the board of directors of the bank subject to the approval of the governor in council.
At the first meeting of the shareholders on January 23, 1935, seven directors were elected for terms to run as follows, one until the third annual general meeting, two until the fourth, two until the fifth, and two until the sixth annual general meeting. Directors must hold at least ten shares of the capital stock of the bank, must be British subjects ordinarily resident in Canada, must not receive remuneration out of public funds in any capacity, and must have no connection with a chartered bank.
There is also an executive committee of the board of directors consisting of the governor, deputy governor, and one member of the board, which must meet once a week. The board itself must meet at least four times a year. The Deputy Minister of Finance is ex-officio a member of the board of directors and of the executive committee, but is without a vote.
The bank commenced business on March 11, 1935, think of it, just a little over a year ago, and has had no time yet to even function. A statement is required of the assets and liabilities of the bank as at the close of business on each Wednesday.
Those are the functions, broadly speaking, of the Bank of Canada, which began to function just a little over a year ago, and it has functioned well, I believe, considering the turmoil and stress which a general election causes all over Canada, and in view of the clamour and agitation there was throughout this country for a change in our banking and monetary system. Our banking system has come down from confederation, down through the dark days of the past five years, and has stood fast against clamour and agitation to change the monetary system. I think the government would have been well advised to give the Bank of Canada one or two more years in which to function, and I believe the people of Canada would prefer that, leaving
Bank of Canada

changes to come about gradually to meet changing conditions in our economic and financial life.
By the resolution now before the committee the government proposes to amend the Bank of Canada Act, and to make it a government ownership institution to the extent of fifty-one per cent. As you know, Mr. Chairman, the Bank of Canada started with a very low capitalization, only S5,000,000, a very small capital indeed, out of which the bank provided for its salaries and kept going. Now the government comes along and says: We are going to go into government ownership, but we are going to have, not one hundred per cent government ownership of the bank as we promised the electors, but only fifty-one per cent. The government says that in this way it will have some control over the Bank of Canada. But what control did it have over the Home Bank? It proposes government ownership to the extent of only fifty-one per cent instead of one hundred per cent. Is there any control over the chartered banks? Let hon. members attend the sittings of the banking and commerce committee and see how much the high court of parliament has to do with the chartered banks and the way they function. The powers of the chartered banks are prescribed by the Bank Act, but the Bank Act is being violated in many spheres of activity.
The Macmillan report at page 98 says that it is not necessary for a central bank to have much capital to start with. This resolution calls for government ownership only in name, and in my opinion it will be found that the directors will be selected in the same way that the employment commission were selected, in the same -way that the railway commission and the members of the tariff board were selected. I remember that ten years ago, when I first came into the house, this matter came up, and Mr. Fielding discussed it. I refer to this because of a remark that was made yesterday. The minister distinctly called the attention of 'the committee to the resolution before the chair, proposing government control to the extent of fifty-one per cent, and he indicated the kind of control. That is a matter which will have to be discussed when the bill is in committee and therefore I shall not refer to it on this occasion.
I shall, however, refer to the statement of the minister that in future there will be bilingual notes instead of some being in English and some in French. I would point out that this upsets the whole practice from confederation to the present time, for Sir John Macdonald,
(Mr. Church.]
Sir Wilfrid Laurier and Mr. Fielding opposed it, and bilingual currency. Why? Because it is inconvenient, and what is more it is not desired by the banking people or by the taxpayers and is against the spirit and letter of the British North America Act. They do not want to have notes of that description going all over the world. I can remember when this matter was discussed in the committee on banking and commerce fourteen years ago. I was not a member of the committee, but in the house I heard section 133 of the British North America Act quoted with reference to the use of French and English in Canada. Are you going to have a note, one side of which will be printed in French and the other in English? The thing would be simply intolerable; it could not be carried out in practice. If French branches of banks in Quebec wished to have some notes in French, a certain number of bills are distributed to the banks as demanded in actual practice but not by statute, for convenience only as now given them, but it has to be left to the good judgment of the banking institutions. This note circulation clause of the Bank of Canada Act is copied from section 60 of the consolidated act of 1934 regarding banks and banking. The principle of that section is copied into the Bank of Canada Act. This matter was not discussed in the election campaign in Ontario because such a change in the note issue in Canada is something which every government since confederation has opposed. Every government in Canada has been opposed to having notes issued in two languages and bilingual currency. I wish to protest against it on behalf of the people whom I represent. I am not speaking for all the people of Ontario but I certainly am speaking for my own constituents. As I say, Sir John A. Macdonald and Sir Wilfrid Laurier and Mr. Fielding as well opposed this proposal in the past. Mr. Fielding, Minister of Finance rose in his place in the banking and -commerce committee and said that the government would not have it; he said that the matter should be left where it was since 1867. When bills printed in French were necessary in practice a few would be printed, he said, but this should not be put into the law. When this provision of the bill comes up in committee I intend to take strong ground against this proposal.
We do not know what is going to become of the Bank of Canada. There is a division among the members supporting the government, and I submit that the resolution ought to be withdrawn and held over until next year. I see there is a suggestion that we

Bank of Canada
should come back in the fall. Well, if the government should leave this matter over for a year, it should be left over until next year or the year after, along with other bills with which the government is not yet ready to deal. It would be better to have a Bank of Canada constituted along the lines suggested by the commission of experts who went into the whole situation and that it be given a five year break, one or two of whom submitted a dissenting report. In years to come there may be necessity for a change, but I do not think that time will come in the next five or ten years. I hope the government will give this resolution further consideration and let it stand over. We know what to expect if this is to be anything like the proposal in connection with the British North America Act; we know what the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Spence) said in that regard. I predict the same thing with respect to this resolution, and I am sure the people of Canada will protest against this proposal with regard to bilingual notes. If the proposal were submitted to the people of Ontario the government would not have five members from that province sitting on the treasury benches.

The majority of the members of this house as well as the majority of the people of Canada are fully convinced that monetary reform is essential if we are to have a permanent solution of the economic problem. I would point out that the government will be judged, not on the number of shares they happen to own in the central bank but on the policy which they put into operation. The ownership of the central bank will undoubtedly be a step forward, a step that has been a long time coming, and one that is important, inasmuch as it gives the government control over the issue of credit. Just as the people of Canada expected to have control of credit through parliament, the people of the provinces expect to have control of their credit through provincial banks. I realize that, when reforms in our social and economic life are being discussed or attempted to be made, constitutional difficulties may arise, and it is the duty of the provincial governments and the federal government to cooperate to the limit to bring about these necessary reforms. I suggest to the government that they give authority to the provincial governments to have their own banks in order to make available to the people of the provinces the credit necessary to handle purely provincial matters, so that industry may be assisted in the provinces, prices
regulated, and the economic security of the people guaranteed in so far as the provinces are able to guarantee them. I believe that with the government owned central bank and with provineially owned banks in the various provinces cooperating, economic security for the people of Canada can be effected.
Much has been said in favour of 100 per cent ownership of the national bank, and I believe it should be so. I do not think any small percentage of the people should have a special privilege in relation to the credit of the dominion. I do not believe that they would be left out of the picture when we consider the benefits which will accrue to them as well as to all other citizens of Canada from a properly constituted central bank. They would benefit as well as the rest, and I do not feel that they should have any special privileges granted them, such as 44 per cent, in connection with which we might effect a considerable saving.
References have been made to credit-how it has been created and how it should be manipulated, whether the granting of loans creates deposits and the repayment of loans destroys them. We have heard a good deal about this lately. But wherever money is created it should be created in sufficient quantities, I submit, actually to reflect our real ability to create and distribute wealth. We should see that that is the case in the Dominion of Canada. If we do not have sufficient, or if there is too much, that can be regulated. One hon. member suggested this afternoon that there is more credit available than the dominion can possibly use. He mentioned the figure of $1,400,000,000, and he said that there is not sufficient security behind the people who desire money to-day. We believe that there is sufficient security. We believe that the natural resources of the Dominion of Canada and the willingness of people to apply themselves to those natural resources should be sufficient credit. I do not blame men who to-day, under the system of private control of credit, refuse to grant to industry the money necessary for development. Knowing the position of the markets in this country at the present time, I would not condemn the man who would hesitate to invest his capital in the coal mines of western Canada, where we have fourteen per cent of the entire coal deposits of the world, along with many thousands of people without sufficient coal to keep themselves warm in winter time. But because those people have not the purchasing power to buy coal after it is produced, I would not blame anyone for not investing in projects of coal development.
Judges Act Amendment

So this question of credit and of its control is very important. The question whether it should be controlled absolutely by the federal government or whether it should be decentralized to allow the provinces to have control of their own credit for purely provincial matters is one that should be considered, and I am disappointed that the amendment of the hon. member for Vaneouver-Burrard (Mr. McGeer) was not accepted. I believe that the whole matter of money and credit should be discussed, so that there will be no more mystery in the public mind about it. These doctrines and ideas that are circulating in Canada should be thoroughly analyzed and the truth made known to the people, and I feel sure that until that is done these matters will continue to be seriously debated in this house.

The whole procedure is

On the other hand, I have known men in this country who did quite a large amount of business without actually keeping books, and they did not keep books in some cases not because of any ulterior motive or purpose. It is the government's responsibility if they want to make this an offence punishable by imprisonment, but I can only say that it strikes me as being a very unusual attitude for a Liberal government, judging by what I have heard of them in the past.

I respectfully differ from the hon. gentleman. It says:
